This summer was not what I expected. What was supposed to be a season of flying, freedom, and adventure quickly turned into one of the most challenging times of my life. In one heartbreaking moment, I lost a close friend and discovered that the heart of my airplane — 23U, the Cessna 172 that means so much to me — was broken and in need of a new engine.

This video isn’t just about airplanes or engines. It’s about loss, healing, community, and finding a way forward. From private memorials to the Valdez STOL competition, from the wild bear country of Alaska to picking up a brand-new engine, I’ve been learning what it means to keep moving forward — not moving on.

In this episode, you’ll see:
✈️ The story of how 23U (Cessna 172) needed a new engine.
✈️ Emotional reflections on loss, resilience, and healing through flying.
✈️ Adventures at the Valdez STOL competition — a tradition in Alaska aviation.
✈️ A bear-viewing trip in Alaska, honoring the legacy of a friend and pilot.
✈️ The moment we brought home the new Stoots Aviation IO-370 engine.
✈️ Community, friendship, and what it means to rebuild from broken.

Flying has always been more than nuts and bolts. It’s a passion, a profession, and sometimes a lifeline. Aviation connects us to something bigger — to each other, to healing, and to the skies that still call us upward even when life feels heavy.

If you’re a pilot, aviation enthusiast, or someone who just loves a story of hope and perseverance, this video is for you.

title: You Have to Hear This Engine!
description:
There are moments in aviation that divide the “before” and “after.” For me, this is one of those moments. After eight long months on the ground, my 1963 Cessna 172D — affectionately known as 23 Uniform (N2423U) — finally roared back to life with a brand-new Continental IO-370 engine.

23 Uniform isn’t just an airplane. She’s been my classroom, my teaching partner, and the heart of Angle of Attack, our aviation education company here in Homer, Alaska. For years, she’s trained students, appeared in videos, and carried dreams skyward. But eventually, her old Continental O-300D had enough. When the oil leaks turned serious and the compression dropped, it was time to make a decision — overhaul the old or step boldly into the future.

After a lot of research and soul-searching, I partnered with Stoots Aviation to upgrade to a Continental Prime IO-370-DA3A, a 180-horsepower fuel-injected engine. It’s a modern heartbeat for a timeless airplane. This isn’t just about power — it’s about reliability, performance, and safety. The IO-370 gives new life to the 172D, allowing it to climb stronger, fly smoother, and keep training pilots for decades to come.

The rebuild wasn’t easy. Every nut, bolt, and line had to be touched. My friend and mechanic Dave spent countless hours ensuring every fitting, wire, and torque was perfect. We reshaped the baffling, aligned the spinner, sourced a new airbox, and installed a Sensenich fixed-pitch prop to match the new engine. We even prepped for a Garmin GI-275 Engine Indication System (EIS) to give us precision monitoring on every future flight.

And Alaska didn’t make it easy. Cold mornings, short days, parts delays — but we kept pushing. Every hour in that hangar brought us closer to hearing her heartbeat again.

When the day finally came, we rolled 23U out into the October chill. My son Apollo stood by my side, my family bundled up nearby, and my friend Wes stood watch with a fire extinguisher. Dave and I briefed everything: safety checks, hand signals, shutdown procedures. We were ready.

Dave turned the key.

The propeller spun, the fuel caught, and that beautiful IO-370 came alive. The deep, confident hum filled the air. Oil pressure rose. Temps stabilized. No leaks. No drama. Just pure, steady life.

It’s hard to describe the emotion in that moment. Tomorrow marks six months since I lost my friend Daniel, and hearing that engine start again felt like something inside me healed. After everything — the work, the setbacks, the loss — hearing 23 Uniform run again wasn’t just mechanical; it was spiritual.

After the run, we pushed her into the sunlight, snow-capped mountains framing the moment. She looked perfect — classic skin, modern heart. I snapped a photo with my family and the crew who made it possible. That picture means everything to me.

Now begins the next phase: the engine break-in, the paperwork, and eventually, the first flight. We’ll monitor every number through the GI-275, follow Continental’s procedures, and do it the right way — safely, methodically, patiently.

To everyone who’s supported this journey — the Alpha Squad, the Angle of Attack Angels, my students, and the aviation community — thank you. You made this possible.

This project reminded me why I love aviation: because it challenges us, humbles us, and connects us. It teaches patience and discipline, and when you finally succeed, it gives you a joy that can’t be explained — only felt.

23 Uniform’s new IO-370 isn’t just an engine. It’s a heartbeat. A second chance. A symbol of why we fly.

From Homer, Alaska — thank you for being part of this journey.
Throttle on, my friends.
— Chris Palmer

Buckle up for an unforgettable cross-country flight across the stunning Kenai Peninsula in Alaska! In this 40-minute video, we dive deep into the world of flight training as we follow student pilot Sienna on her longest and most challenging journey yet, flying a Cessna 172 under the guidance of a Master CFI from Angle of Attack Flight School in Homer, Alaska. This isn’t just a scenic joyride—it’s a real-world pilot training adventure packed with aviation lessons, breathtaking Alaska scenery, and the raw beauty of the Harding Ice Field.  

We begin at Homer Airport, where Sienna takes command for a northwest departure along the coast toward Kenai. You’ll see her master radio communication, manage the Cessna 172’s engine with precision (think mixture leaning and RPM adjustments), and nail a smooth landing on Runway 20 Right—all key skills in private pilot training. Along the way, we explore practical aviation tips: why activating a flight plan is a safety must, how to lean the mixture for efficiency, and the art of maintaining airspeed during descent. The flight instructor breaks it all down, making this a goldmine for anyone curious about learning to fly.  

After a fuel stop in Kenai (with a surprise DC-6 cameo!), we soar over the vibrant Kenai Lake, navigating valleys with towering peaks on either side. Sienna learns to read wind patterns for mountain flying, sticking to the windward side to avoid downdrafts—a critical lesson in flight safety. Fog blocks our original plan to land in Seward, so we adapt, climbing to 8,000 feet for a jaw-dropping detour over the Harding Ice Field, the largest contiguous ice field in the U.S. The bright blue pools and wind-sculpted glaciers are unreal—perfect for fans of Alaska landscapes and aerial photography.  

This flight showcases the heart of general aviation: decision-making, adaptability, and the thrill of flying over rugged terrain. Whether you’re an aspiring pilot dreaming of your pilot license, a seasoned aviator brushing up on flight maneuvers, or just here for the Alaska adventures, there’s something for everyone. From preflight planning to handling mountain wave turbulence, we cover it all—plus stunning views of glaciers, lakes, and the wild Kenai Peninsula. title: Letting Students Reset — Then Try Again #flighttraining #flying #groundschool #studentpilot
description:
Most of the time, I let my student pilots fly the airplane — that’s how they learn best. But sometimes, it helps to step in. In this Cessna 172, I take the controls for a moment so Sienna can reset, breathe, and see what a stable approach looks and feels like without all the pressure.

This gives her a mental model to emulate on her next few landings — the sight picture, the pace, and the coordination. It’s a great teaching reset that builds confidence instead of stress. title: Why Good Instructors Stay Quiet #flighttraining #aviation #flying #groundschool #studentpilot
description:

As an instructor, it’s tempting to jump in, but silence gives space for learning. I offer light guidance here and there, showing her how minor adjustments to pitch, power, and sight picture can bring everything together. This is real flight training — where the student starts taking ownership and truly begins learning to fly.

title: Well, this sucks!
description:

On a recent flight, we started seeing some unusual temperature readings in the engine—nothing catastrophic, but enough to raise an eyebrow. After run-up, a closer inspection revealed something we didn’t want to see… buildup inside one of the cylinders.

title: Always Fly IN TRIM — The Secret to Smooth Flight #flighttraining #flying #groundschool #studentpilot
description:
One of the most misunderstood parts of flying is staying in trim — at all times. In this Cessna 172, I’m showing Sienna, my student pilot, how to build the habit of trimming the airplane in every attitude we fly.

At first, you hold the control pressure with muscle, then trim it off, and finally make small visual adjustments to keep the airplane perfectly balanced. Being properly trimmed means the airplane flies hands-off and stable, leaving your brain free to think ahead.

Flying in trim is one of those simple-but-crucial habits every pilot must master — a cornerstone of smooth, confident flight training, and essential for great private pilot training and safe learning to fly.

title: Morning Meeting
description:
If you want the lesson plan, writing template, and sensory links comment “morning meeting” and I’ll DM you! 


This is a simple morning meeting routine that I do with my students a few times a month. Students create their own “Today I Feel” writing page with a picture of themselves showing their feeling AND a speech balloon stating something they would say when they felt that way.

title: Ocean of potential, a sea of possibilities | Pamela Lee | TEDxSt Helier
description: Pamela argues that our world is leaving vast oceans of human potential unexplored, especially when it comes to girls and women in sport. She asks what happens when half the world is prepared to be perfect, while the other half is trained to be brave. From the helm of a high performance offshore racing yacht, where there is no men’s or women’s category and the sea only rewards skill and endurance. She explores how sport can be one of the most powerful engines of human potential. It builds courage, decision making, resilience, and leadership – yet most girls are never given the same structure, investment, or belief as boys. The talk connects big picture themes of equality, representation, and social change with Pamela’s lived experience: an equal childhood, unequal systems, and a career breaking records in one of the most male dominated arenas on earth. It is a call to use sport as a platform for empowerment and to stop treating women’s potential like the deep ocean: acknowledged, but underused and underestimated. An Irish offshore sailor, ocean racer, and world record holder based in Brittany, France. Pamela grew up on Ireland’s east coast, where time on the water sparked a lifelong drive for adventure, performance, and independence. She has built an accomplished career in elite offshore racing, earning three world records around Ireland and gaining deep experience in solo, short- handed, and crewed campaigns across the Atlantic and in the French offshore circuit. In 2022, she founded Ripple Racing, a high-performance offshore racing company. In 2025, she launched #EmpowHer, a campaign designed to use sailing as a platform for equality, visibility, and greater female participation in sport and maritime careers. She is a passionate advocate for social change through sport, believing that representation matters and that women belong at every level of competition, leadership, and opportunity. She continues to race, build, and speak with the goal of opening doors for the next generation. description:
我们习惯把旧物称为“废弃物”，但如果重新审视它们，废弃是否真的意味着失去价值？一件由废旧瓦楞纸制作而成的精美器物，打开了可持续设计师张婕对于“升级再造”的探索。升级再造，不只是简单的回收，而是通过设计赋予旧材料新的价值：让废旧矿泉水瓶成为时尚产品，让旧家具重新进入生活，让被遗忘的物品获得新的可能。从全球可持续设计研究，到带领学生探索废弃材料的创新应用，再到推动升级再造走进社区与公众生活，张婕始终相信，设计不仅改变物品的形态，也改变人们看待价值的方式。当我们重新设计一件被丢弃的物品时，我们重新思考的其实是：什么值得被保留，什么值得被珍惜。升级再造并不一定需要宏大的行动，每一次对旧物的重新利用，每一个微小的创造，都可能成为改变世界的一部分。 北京林业大学艺术设计学院副教授，德国红点奖（Red Dot Design Award）获得者，长期从事可持续设计研究、教学与实践，关注设计如何影响日常行为，并回应环境与社会挑战。

When Two Kids Trigger Each Other (Try This!) #studentbehavior #classroomenvironment
description:
When two kids constantly trigger each other, it’s not because they’re “bad together.”
It’s usually a mix of low regulation, skill needs, too much access and not enough structure.

How to handle it:

Add distance with purpose:
Don’t just separate, give each child a role, job, or different activity.

Reduce unstructured time:
Transitions and free play are where this shows up most. Add visual choices or clear time limits.

Move the body:
Walks, heavy work, races, or carrying items help reset nervous systems fast.

 Coach after calm:
Problem-solve later, not in the moment. Teach what to do next time when emotions are down.

 Reintroduce slowly:
They don’t need unlimited access to each other. Short, successful interactions build skills.

This isn’t about control.
It’s about supporting regulation and teaching skills.
